slides.title: The vault under creator banking
slides.subtitle: Your credentials, your connections, your rules.
slides.presenter: Samuel Vieira · Business Development · October 2026 · Strictly confidential
slides.notes: You have an RFP open for a token vault, and you told us where the product is going: one creator account on top, several banks, issuers and transfer providers underneath. This deck answers the vault question and the question you asked us most, which is who decides where each creator lands. Every claim in it is labeled with its basis, so your payments team can check it without us in the room.

items.title: WHAT THE VAULT HAS TO HOLD

slides.title: Why we are here
slides.sub: An RFP for a token vault, and a design that needs more than one.

slides.kicker: WHY WE ARE HERE · THE ANSWER UP FRONT
slides.headline: A vault stores the credential. Your design also needs a layer that decides where it goes. Yuno does both; here is how far each goes today.
slides.source: Nine things your design needs: item by item on slide 45, vendor by vendor on slides 46 and 47. Competitor lines from public pages, read 7 October 2026.

tiles.label: WHERE YUNO LEADS
tiles.caption: Routing rules for card payments, processor integrations already built, a banking API across providers, and payouts.

tiles.label: LEVEL
tiles.caption: A card vault at PCI DSS Level 1 with hosted capture. All three of us have one.

tiles.label: WHERE VGS AND BASIS THEORY LEAD
tiles.caption: Network token depth, token types for personal data, issued-card display (PIN setting at Basis Theory), and a more established proxy with custom code.

slides.bar: **In one line.** If the RFP is for storage alone, a standalone vault is a fair choice. If the vault has to serve a multi-bank, multi-issuer product, the harder half is the layer above it.
slides.notes: Here is the conclusion before the detail. We compared Yuno with VGS and Basis Theory on nine things your design needs. On four of them a standalone vault leads today, and we say so. On one we are level. On four Yuno leads, and those four are the ones your architecture adds on top of a vault: routing rules for card payments, processor integrations that are already built, a banking API across providers, and payouts. Where any of these is only partly there today, the deck says so.

slides.kicker: WHY WE ARE HERE · HOW TO READ THIS DECK
slides.headline: Every capability claim carries one of three labels, so your team can check it without us in the room.

cards.title: Not yet confirmed in writing inside Yuno
cards.body: Shown with an owner, never as a fact. The six open items are listed together on slide 50. In the appendix, Not in docs marks a gap in our public reference.

slides.bar: **Why it matters.** A vault sits under everything you build on it. We would rather show you an open item today than have your engineers find it in the sandbox.
slides.notes: We label every claim. Confirmed means it is in our public documentation, and most of it can be tried in the sandbox: the proxy sandbox is open today, while the cryptogram API and the account updater are switched on for your organization. Public docs means we read it on a competitor's own pages and you should confirm it with them. Open means we have not confirmed it in writing internally, so we will not present it as a fact. A vault is the wrong place for surprises.

slides.notes: The comparison row by row. Rows two to five are where VGS and Basis Theory lead today, and we would rather you hear it from us: deeper network token programs, a more established proxy with custom code, token types built for personal data, and tooling to show an issued card, plus PIN setting at Basis Theory. The next two slides take each vendor on its own. Rows six to nine are what your architecture adds on top of a vault, and that is where Yuno leads. The competitor columns come from their public pages on 7 October; where a cell says something was not found, we mean on those pages, so please confirm with them.

slides.kicker: THE PATH FORWARD · WHAT WE OWE YOU
slides.headline: Six open items, each with an owner and a written answer in our RFP response.
rows: Tables you define for identity and customer records, and how bank and entity data is stored and accessed: availability and API reference
Banking as a service puts far more than cards in the vault.
Rule-based allocation of creators across banks and issuers
It turns "who decides" from code you maintain into a rule you set.
US banking and issuing providers connected today, their policy for your category, and one entity on several connections
No single bank should be able to cut a creator off. That depends on which banks are behind the API.
Token requestor model for each card network, scheme activation per network, and export of network transaction IDs, bank and entity data
Together they decide what you can take with you if you ever change vault.
Contractual uptime, failover design, rate limits and the subprocessor list
A vault in the payment path must never be the weak point.
Stablecoin conversion providers
Yield on balances is part of your design, and outside the vault itself.
slides.notes: These are the six things we have not confirmed in writing, collected in one place. Each has an owning team at Yuno, and each gets a written answer with our RFP response. If any of them is a deciding factor for you, tell us now and we will answer it first.
